newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr sulks as RBA prolongs agony.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr sulks as RBA prolongs agony.

text.p: The Australian dollar subsided to a soft close Wednesday after supporters found the Reserve Bank's silence a surprisingly uncomfortable one.

The currency had been losing ground for weeks on speculation the central bank would ease following its monthly board meeting Tuesday, so the lack of a cut should have bolstered sentiment. However, analysts felt a move could still come at any time so today's reprieve was seen as merely prolonging the agony.
"We still lean to the view they will ease again and until that uncertainty is resolved the dollar will be under pressure," said Michael Workman, currency economist at Commonwealth Bank.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had subsided to US$0.7626/31 having briefly touching US$0.7650 when it became clear the RBA would not be easing today.

That was off its opening US$0.7634/39 and Tuesday's late US$0.7650/55 suggesting the market was neither too short nor inclined to give the dollar the benefit of the doubt when it came to the risk of a rate cut.

Traders still nurse painful memories of the last easing on December 11 which came a week after a board meeting. Those scars meant the market could not relax even if analysts felt policy was likely to be on hold until the next meeting on March 4.

The market has been discounting a rate cut for more than a month as a run of data confirmed both that inflation was low and falling and the economy slowed sharply last quarter. So when the RBA held its first board meeting of the year on Tuesday, many felt it would respond with the fourth easing since July.
The bank's silence, therefore, suggested it was not as gloomy on the economy as some other commentators and perhaps still harboured concerns about inflation and wages.
Some, for instance, suspected the RBA was waiting for Thursday's release of wages data for the November quarter and if these confirmed a slowing trend it might ease on Friday morning.
Forecasts are for annual earnings growth to dip to 3.6 percent from 3.8 percent the quarter before, comfortably below the RBA's danger zone of 4.5-5.0 percent.

Others felt the bank could move if the January employment data in a week's time showed no improvement or if Q4 business investment on February 27 revealed a slackening in previously strong investment intentions.

Thus while most analysts might reckon a cut was off the agenda until the next board meeting on March 4, the market would be watching the screens every day just in case. And it would be hard for the dollar to sustain a rally in such an atmosphere.

"I think people still want to test the 76 cent level," said CBA's Workman. "The technical background is pretty bearish and once we're through this US$0.7590/7600 area there is little in the way of support until 75 cents."

Interim support was put at US$0.7720, while resistance had been evident at US$0.7660 and analysts reckoned the currency would have to recapture the distant US$0.7735 to sap the momentum from its two-month old downtrend.
The outlook was markedly different on most crosses, however, since domestic rates would be attractive compared to those in much of Europe and Japan whether they were cut again or not.

That yield cushion kept the local currency firm at 93.85/95 yen and 1.2572/84 marks from 93.70/80 and 1.2516/32 late Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it softened a touch to 58.3 from a previous 58.4 finish.

Elsewhere, the market would be keeping a wary eye on today's conclusion of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting. The Fed is widely expected to keep rates steady but there is a small risk it could hike as a pre-emptive strike against inflation.
In such a case, dealers expected the local currency to come under stiff pressure against the US$ as the yield differential between the two narrowed. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
